title: Understanding Heat and Temperature
subject: Science
description: What heat is, its natural and artificial sources, how heat moves (touch, moving matter, empty space), conductors and insulators, heat vs temperature, body temperature, everyday temperatures, seasons, farming and absolute zero.

questions.question: Heat is a form of ___.
questions.explanation: The book begins by saying that heat is a form of energy — the energy that makes things feel warm or hot.

questions.question: Every object around us is made of tiny particles that are too small to see. The book calls these particles:
questions.explanation: The book says every object is made of tiny particles called molecules, which are always moving and bumping into each other.

questions.question: What are the tiny particles inside every object always doing?
questions.explanation: The particles are always moving, always vibrating and bumping into each other — even in cold objects.

questions.question: The faster the particles of an object move, the ___ the object gets.
questions.explanation: Faster-moving particles carry more energy, and more energy means the object is hotter.

questions.question: Two identical iron balls are at the same temperature, but one is much bigger. Which contains more heat energy?
options: the bigger ball, because it has more particles
the smaller ball, because it is packed tighter
both the same, because the temperature is equal
neither, because iron cannot hold heat
questions.explanation: The book says the more particles an object has, the more heat energy it contains. The bigger ball has more particles, so more heat — even at the same temperature.

questions.question: In a block of ice, the tiny particles have stopped moving completely.
questions.explanation: False. Even in a block of ice every particle is still moving, just very slowly. The colder something gets, the slower its particles move.

questions.question: The colder something gets, the slower its particles move.
questions.explanation: True. Cold objects have slow-moving particles; hot objects have fast-moving particles.

questions.question: In which of these would the particles be moving the slowest?
questions.explanation: Colder objects have slower particles. Ice is the coldest item listed, so its particles move the slowest.

questions.question: When you feel warmth from sunlight on a winter morning, how does that heat reach your skin?
options: through the ground under your feet
only after the clouds pass it on
along copper wires from the Sun
questions.explanation: The book says the Sun's heat reaches you 'without any wire or something carrying it' — it travels through empty space.

questions.question: After rubbing your palms together hard for 15 seconds, your cheeks feel warm when you press your palms on them. Why?
options: your palms pulled cold out of your cheeks
blood stopped flowing to your hands
questions.explanation: Rubbing two surfaces together creates friction, and friction produces heat. The warm palms then pass that heat to your cheeks.

questions.question: Predict: after rubbing a pencil eraser back and forth very fast on paper for 20 seconds, the eraser will feel
questions.explanation: Fast rubbing creates friction, which generates heat, so the eraser warms up — just like your palms did.

questions.question: Select ALL the statements about heat that the book says are true.
options: Heat is a form of energy.
Faster-moving particles make an object hotter.
Heat can be seen clearly with our eyes.
Particles stop moving in any cold object.
questions.explanation: Heat is energy carried by moving particles, and faster particles mean a hotter object. We cannot see heat (only feel it), and even cold particles keep moving, just slowly.

questions.question: Why does a hot object have more energy than the SAME object when it is cold?
questions.explanation: The number of particles in the same object has not changed. What changed is the speed of the particles — faster particles carry more energy.

questions.question: People named and measured heat long before any living creature depended on it.
questions.explanation: False. The book says the opposite: long before anyone gave heat a name or measured it, every living creature on Earth already depended on it to survive.

questions.question: Which of these can we NOT do with heat, according to the book?
questions.explanation: The book says we cannot see heat or hold it, but we can feel it, generate it and measure it (as temperature).

questions.question: The book says 'the more energy the particles carry, the hotter the object gets'. Which everyday change shows particles gaining energy?
options: ice staying frozen in a freezer
water in a kettle warming up
questions.explanation: Only the kettle water is getting hotter, which means its particles are moving faster and carrying more energy. The others are cooling or staying cold.

questions.question: Which of the following is the greatest natural source of heat for the Earth?
questions.explanation: The Sun is the greatest natural source of heat for our planet; all life on Earth depends on its warmth.

questions.question: Just like light, heat has two kinds of sources. They are:
questions.explanation: Heat sources are either natural (occurring on their own) or artificial (human-made).

questions.question: Which animals generate heat from within their own bodies?
questions.explanation: Mammals and birds make heat inside their bodies as a natural result of their life processes.

questions.question: Fish, frogs and lizards get most of their body heat from
questions.explanation: These animals do not make much heat themselves; they absorb it from warm rocks, sunlight and water around them.

questions.question: A lizard would most likely warm itself by
options: lying on a warm rock in the sun
questions.explanation: Lizards absorb heat from their surroundings — warm rocks, sunlight and water — rather than producing it inside.

questions.question: All living creatures make their own body heat.
questions.explanation: False. All living creatures carry body heat, but not all make it themselves. Fish, frogs and lizards absorb heat from their surroundings.

questions.question: A bolt of lightning generates heat hotter than the surface of the Sun.
questions.explanation: True. The book says a bolt of lightning generates enormous heat, hotter than the surface of the Sun.

questions.question: Lightning can naturally start
questions.explanation: Lightning can start forest fires, which the book describes as natural heat events.

questions.question: A forest fire started by a lightning strike is an example of
questions.explanation: Nobody made the fire — lightning started it on its own — so it is a natural heat event.

questions.question: The thermal camera image in the book shows
options: heat given off by human bodies
questions.explanation: The caption says the thermal camera is detecting the heat naturally generated by human bodies.

questions.question: Select ALL the natural sources of heat.
questions.explanation: The Sun and lightning occur on their own, so they are natural. Gas stoves and electric ovens are human-made (artificial).

questions.question: According to the book, where does ALL heat ultimately come from?
questions.explanation: The book says all heat ultimately comes from energy being released or transferred.

questions.question: The book compares the sources of heat with the sources of which other thing?
questions.explanation: It says 'Just like light, heat has both natural and human-made (artificial) sources.'

questions.question: Which statement about living bodies as a heat source is correct?
options: fish make heat by burning fuel inside them
lizards make heat even without any sunlight
mammals make heat as a result of their life processes
frogs make heat by vibrating flight muscles
questions.explanation: Only mammals and birds generate heat from within. Frogs, fish and lizards absorb heat from their surroundings.

questions.question: All life on Earth depends on the warmth the Sun provides.
questions.explanation: True. The book states that all life on Earth depends on the warmth the Sun provides.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a natural source of heat?
questions.explanation: A campfire is created by humans, so it is an artificial source. The others occur on their own.

questions.question: The heat deep inside the Earth is called
questions.explanation: 'Geothermal' means heat from the Earth — the very hot interior of our planet.

questions.question: The city of Beppu in Japan has over how many hot springs?
questions.explanation: The book says Beppu has over 2,000 hot springs, with hot water and steam coming up from deep underground.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a use of hot-spring heat mentioned for the people of Beppu?
questions.explanation: The book lists cooking, bathing and warming homes as uses of Beppu's free heat. Running cars is not mentioned.

questions.question: Hot water shooting up out of the ground is called a
questions.explanation: A geyser is hot water shooting up from the ground; a hot spring is a natural pool of warm water.

questions.question: A natural pool of warm water is called a
questions.explanation: The book defines hot springs as natural pools of warm water.

questions.question: Volcanoes are an everyday source of usable geothermal energy.
questions.explanation: False. Volcanoes ARE sources of geothermal energy, but the book says they are not an everyday source of usable geothermal energy.

questions.question: Puga Valley, where India's geothermal heat escapes through hot springs, is in
questions.explanation: In Puga Valley, Ladakh, heat trapped inside the Earth escapes naturally through hot springs and geysers.

questions.question: ONGC stands for
questions.explanation: ONGC is the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation, which is building India's first geothermal energy project.

questions.question: What is the aim of ONGC's project in Puga Valley?
options: pipe hot water all the way to Delhi homes
cool the whole valley in summer
bottle the spring water to sell
questions.explanation: ONGC is building India's first geothermal energy project to turn the underground heat into clean electricity.

questions.question: India's first geothermal energy project is being built at
questions.explanation: Puga Valley in Ladakh is the site of India's first geothermal energy project.

questions.question: On the floor of the Pacific Ocean, boiling hot water shoots from cracks in a place where
questions.explanation: These vents are in complete darkness on the ocean floor, where no sunlight has ever reached.

questions.question: Creatures living around deep-sea vents get their warmth from
options: warm currents flowing down from above
heat coming from inside the Earth
questions.explanation: The book asks where the heat comes from — it is geothermal heat from the Earth's interior, since no sunlight reaches there and the surface warmth never reaches the bottom.

questions.question: Most of the ocean floor stays freezing cold even though the surface water above it is much warmer.
questions.explanation: True. Apart from a few hot vents, most of the ocean floor is freezing cold, and the surface warmth never reaches the bottom.

questions.question: In which three forms does the Earth's inner heat show up at the surface, according to the book?
questions.explanation: Geothermal heat sometimes comes to the surface as hot springs, geysers and volcanoes.

questions.question: The hot springs of Puga Valley are heated by sunlight trapped between the mountains.
questions.explanation: False. They are heated by heat trapped deep inside the Earth (geothermal energy) escaping to the surface.

questions.question: Why is the heat used in Beppu described as 'free'?
options: the government pays for all of it
it is made by giant solar panels
it comes from burning dry wood
questions.explanation: Hot water and steam come up from deep underground on their own, so people use this heat without producing it.

questions.question: Gas stoves and campfires produce heat by
questions.explanation: All human-made fires, like gas stoves and campfires, produce heat by burning fuel.

questions.question: Fire counts as an ARTIFICIAL source of heat when
options: a volcano throws out hot lava
the Sun heats up a dark rock
humans make it for cooking or warmth
questions.explanation: Fire can be natural (lightning, forest fires) or artificial — when humans make it for cooking, warmth and so on.

questions.question: When you rub your hands together, the heat is created by
questions.explanation: Friction between the two rubbing surfaces creates heat.

questions.question: Without a matchbox or lighter, campers and hikers start a fire by using
questions.explanation: Campers, hikers and soldiers use friction to create sparks and start a fire in the wild.

questions.question: Our ancestors made fire by
questions.explanation: Rubbing two dry sticks together with enough speed and pressure generated heat through friction.

questions.question: For rubbing sticks to make fire, the sticks had to be rubbed with
questions.explanation: The book says rubbing two dry sticks with enough speed and pressure generated enough heat to ignite dry grass.

questions.question: The heat from rubbing sticks was enough to ignite
questions.explanation: The friction heat was enough to ignite dry grass and make fire.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four benefits of fire shown in the 'Discovery of Fire' box?
questions.explanation: The four benefits shown are: cook food, stay warm in winter, light up darkness and protect from predators.

questions.question: Fire helped early people protect themselves from
questions.explanation: One of the four benefits of fire was protection from predators.

questions.question: Electric heaters, ovens, geysers and room heaters convert
questions.explanation: Electrical appliances turn electrical energy into heat energy.

questions.question: Traditional fire-making by friction is still taught as a survival skill today.
questions.explanation: True. Even today, fire-making by friction is taught as a survival skill in many cultures.

questions.question: Fire can only ever be a natural source of heat.
questions.explanation: False. Fire is natural when started by lightning but artificial when humans make it, e.g. a gas stove or campfire.

questions.question: Which of these is an artificial source of heat?
questions.explanation: A room heater is human-made; lightning, the Sun and volcanoes occur naturally.

questions.question: Which pair contains TWO artificial sources of heat?
options: a gas stove and an electric oven
a lightning bolt and the Sun
a hot spring and a geyser
a volcano and a forest fire
questions.explanation: Gas stoves and electric ovens are human-made. The other pairs are all natural sources.

questions.question: Why did the discovery of fire 'change everything' for early humans?
options: it ended their need for the Sun's warmth
it gave warmth, cooked food, light and safety
it let them measure temperature exactly
it created the first electric heaters
questions.explanation: With fire, people could cook food, stay warm in winter, light up the darkness and protect themselves from predators.

questions.question: A 'geyser' in a bathroom is an electrical appliance, but a geyser in nature is hot water shooting up from the ground.
questions.explanation: True. The book lists electric geysers among electrical appliances, and separately describes natural geysers as hot water shooting up from the ground.

questions.question: In the 'Sort it!' activity you write N or A under each picture. Under a picture of a lit gas stove you should write
options: N, because gas comes from the ground
A, because the stove is metal
A, because people made the fire
N, because fire is always natural
questions.explanation: A gas stove is a human-made (artificial) fire used for cooking, so it is marked A.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: Heat always flows
options: from something cooler to something hotter
only through the air around objects
only through water and other liquids
from something hotter to something cooler
questions.explanation: Heat always moves in one direction: from the hotter object to the cooler one, never the other way around.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: Heat stops flowing between two objects that are touching when
options: the cooler object starts to melt
the air around them stops moving
questions.explanation: Heat flows from hot to cold until both objects reach the same temperature.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: In the investigation, a spoon chilled in ice is placed in a cup of warm water. After a minute the spoon has
questions.explanation: Heat flows from the warm water into the cold spoon, so the spoon warms up.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: In the same investigation, what happens to the warm water while the cold spoon sits in it?
options: it does not change at all
questions.explanation: The water gives some of its heat to the spoon, so the water cools slightly while the spoon warms.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: In the spoon-and-cup investigation, heat travelled
options: from the cool spoon to the warm water
from the cup into the ice
from the ice into the room
from the warm water to the cool spoon
questions.explanation: Heat always moves from the hotter thing (warm water) to the cooler thing (cold spoon).

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: If you waited long enough with the spoon in the cup, you would find that
options: spoon and water reach the same temperature
the spoon becomes hotter than the water
the water turns back into ice
the spoon keeps getting hotter forever
questions.explanation: Heat keeps flowing until both objects are at the same temperature, and then the flow stops.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: Heat can sometimes flow on its own from a cold object to a hot object.
questions.explanation: False. Heat flows from hotter to cooler, never the other way around.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: Heat is always on the move.
questions.explanation: True. The book says heat is always on the move, flowing from hotter to cooler things.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: The three ways in which heat moves are through
questions.explanation: The book describes heat moving through touch, through moving matter and through empty space.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: You drop ice cubes into a glass of juice. In which direction does heat move?
options: from the juice into the ice
from the ice into the juice
questions.explanation: The juice is warmer than the ice, so heat flows from the juice into the ice. That is why the juice gets colder and the ice melts.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: You press your hand on a cold metal bench. What is really happening?
options: coldness flows from the bench into your hand
no heat moves between hand and bench
heat flows from the bench into your hand
heat leaves your hand and goes into the bench
questions.explanation: Heat moves from hot to cold. Your hand is warmer than the bench, so heat flows out of your hand — there is no 'coldness' that flows.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: Which statement about heat flow is NOT true?
options: it can only flow through air
it flows from hot to cold
it stops when temperatures are equal
it never flows from cold to hot
questions.explanation: Heat flows through touch, through moving matter and through empty space — not only through air. The other three statements are correct.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: A metal spoon in the sun gets hot in minutes, yet warm surface water never warms the deep ocean floor. The book uses this to suggest that
options: metal cannot hold any heat for long
heat moves differently in different materials
heat never moves through water at all
sunlight is actually cold near water
questions.explanation: The puzzle leads to the idea that heat travels more easily through some materials (like metal) than others.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: A hot cup of tea left on a table warms the air around it a little as it cools down.
questions.explanation: True. The tea is hotter than the air, so heat flows from the tea to the air until they are at the same temperature.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: Which of these happens when a hot object and a cold object touch?
options: the hot one cools, the cold one warms
questions.explanation: Heat moves from the hotter object to the cooler one, so one cools while the other warms.

questions.question: When two objects are in contact and heat moves directly through the material, heat is moving
questions.explanation: Heat moving through direct contact between objects is heat travelling 'through touch'.

questions.question: Only the tip of a metal spoon is in hot tea, yet the handle soon becomes warm because
options: hot air carried the heat upward
the tea climbed up the spoon
light from the tea warmed the handle
questions.explanation: Heat moved along the metal from the hot end to the cool end.

questions.question: Materials that let heat travel through them easily are called
questions.explanation: Conductors, like metals, let heat pass through them easily.

questions.question: Materials that do NOT let heat pass through easily are called
questions.explanation: Insulators — such as wood, plastic and wool — do not let heat pass through easily.

questions.question: Which of these is a good conductor of heat?
questions.explanation: Metals like steel are conductors. Wood, plastic and wool are insulators.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an insulator of heat?
questions.explanation: Iron is a metal, and metals are conductors. Wood, plastic and wool are insulators.

questions.question: A wooden spoon left in the same hot tea stays cool because
options: wood soaks up all of the hot tea
wood does not pass heat along easily
wood is much colder than the tea
wood floats on top of the hot tea
questions.explanation: Wood is an insulator — it doesn't pass heat energy along as easily as metal does.

questions.question: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon sit in hot soup for the same time. Whose handle feels hotter?
questions.explanation: Metal is a conductor and carries heat up to the handle; wood is an insulator and stays cool.

questions.question: Which material is better for the handle of a cooking pot, and why?
options: metal, because it is a conductor
wood, because it is an insulator
questions.explanation: A handle should stay cool to hold. Wood is an insulator and does not pass heat easily, so it is the better choice.

questions.question: On a cold morning a metal bench feels much colder than a wooden bench, though both have been outside all morning. The best explanation is:
options: heat leaves your hand faster into the metal
the metal bench has a lower temperature
the wooden bench has a higher temperature
the wooden bench gives off its own heat
questions.explanation: Both benches are at the same temperature. Metal conducts heat away from your hand quickly, so it FEELS colder. The book's clue marks this as being about heat, not temperature.

questions.question: Wood and plastic are good at letting heat pass through them quickly.
questions.explanation: False. Wood and plastic are insulators — they do not let heat pass through easily.

questions.question: Wool is an insulator of heat.
questions.explanation: True. The book lists wool with wood and plastic as insulators.

questions.question: Select ALL the insulators.
questions.explanation: Wool and plastic do not let heat pass easily, so they are insulators. Copper and iron are metals — conductors.

questions.question: In the matching exercise, 'Metal' matches with
options: the greatest natural source of heat
lets heat travel through it very easily
does not let heat pass through easily
a device that tells how hot something is
questions.explanation: Metal is a conductor, so it lets heat travel through it very easily.

questions.question: Why do we wear woollen clothes in winter?
options: wool conducts heat into the body
wool keeps body heat from escaping
wool makes its own body heat
questions.explanation: Wool is an insulator: it slows heat leaving the body, helping us conserve our own warmth.

questions.question: If one end of each object is held in hot tea, which would get warm at the other end fastest?
questions.explanation: Steel is a metal and conducts heat quickly along its length. The others are insulators.

questions.question: In the matching exercise, 'Wool / Plastic' matches with
options: does not let heat pass through easily
lets heat travel through very easily
a device that tells how hot something is
questions.explanation: Wool and plastic are insulators — they do not let heat pass through easily.

questions.question: A metal pan heats food quickly, but its metal handle can burn you. Which ONE property explains both facts?
questions.explanation: Because metal conducts heat easily, it passes heat into the food quickly — and just as easily into the handle and your hand.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: When air is heated, it
questions.explanation: Heated air rises, and cooler air from the surroundings rushes in to take its place.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: When warm air rises, the cooler air around it
options: rushes in to take its place
questions.explanation: Cooler air moves in to fill the space left by rising warm air, forming a loop.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: The paper spiral held above a candle spins because
options: hot air rising from the candle pushes it
the candle flame touches the paper
cold air falls down onto the spiral
the thread slowly twists on its own
questions.explanation: Heated air above the flame rises, cooler air rushes in, and this moving loop of air makes the spiral spin.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: When water at the bottom of a pot is heated, it
questions.explanation: Heated water rises to the top and cooler water moves down to take its place.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: The loop of rising warm water and sinking cool water carries warmth
questions.explanation: This loop keeps repeating and carries warmth through the whole pot of water.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: Heat travelling 'through moving matter' happens in materials that can flow, such as
questions.explanation: The book's examples are heated air rising and heated water rising — both are matter that can move and flow.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: The spiral activity should be done away from
questions.explanation: Moving air from windows and fans would spin the spiral and spoil the test, so do it away from them.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: In the spiral activity, the spiral must be kept well above the flame and never touch it.
questions.explanation: True. The instructions say to keep the spiral well above the flame and always ask an adult.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: The paper spiral spins because the thread is heated and shrinks.
questions.explanation: False. The spiral spins because hot air rising from the candle moves past it in a loop with cooler air rushing in.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: Hot air from a heater rises to the ceiling and cooler air rushes in until the whole room is warm. Heat is moving
questions.explanation: Air moving in a loop (warm up, cool in) is heat travelling through moving matter.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: The Sun's heat reaches the Earth
questions.explanation: The Sun is millions of kilometres away; its heat travels through empty space as rays (radiation).

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: Heat from the Sun does NOT need ___ to carry it to us.
questions.explanation: The book says the Sun's heat doesn't touch us and doesn't need air to carry it — it travels as rays through empty space.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: You stand near a campfire on a cold night and your face feels warm even though the air between is cold. Heat is moving
questions.explanation: The warmth reaches you as rays without touching the flames and without warm air carrying it — that is heat through empty space (radiation).

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: Heat that travels as rays is called
questions.explanation: The book says heat from the Sun travels through empty space as rays (radiation).

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: Blowing on hot soup cools it down because
options: the air adds more heat to the soup
moving air carries heat away from the soup
your breath is colder than ice cubes
questions.explanation: The soup is hotter than your breath, so heat flows from the soup into the moving air, which carries it away.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: Blowing on your cold hands warms them because
options: your breath is colder than your hands
your breath is warmer than your hands
questions.explanation: Heat flows from hot to cold. Your warm breath is hotter than your cold hands, so it gives them heat — the opposite of the soup case.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: Select ALL the examples of heat moving through MOVING MATTER.
options: water rising to the top of a heated pot
warm air rising to a room's ceiling
a spoon handle warming in tea
questions.explanation: Rising water and rising air are moving matter. Sunlight is heat through empty space; the spoon is heat through touch.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: Which statement about heat travelling through empty space is TRUE?
options: it reaches us with nothing carrying it
it needs a solid metal path to follow
it needs air around it to move through
it only works inside liquid water
questions.explanation: Radiation crosses empty space; the Sun's heat reaches us without air or any material carrying it.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: The Sun millions of kilometres away and a campfire a few steps away both warm you in the same way. That way is heat through
questions.explanation: In both cases the warmth reaches you as rays without contact and without warm air carrying it.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: Air that is heated becomes lighter and rises, which is why the spiral spins.
questions.explanation: True. Heated air rises and cooler air rushes in; this loop of moving air spins the spiral.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: Dark-coloured objects
questions.explanation: Dark objects absorb more sunlight and usually become hotter.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: Light-coloured objects
questions.explanation: Light-coloured objects reflect sunlight, so they stay cooler.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: On a sunny day, which shirt feels hotter?
questions.explanation: The black shirt absorbs more sunlight and becomes hotter; the white one reflects it.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: In the thermal image, the darker shirts glow
questions.explanation: Red and orange show more heat; lighter shirts stay cool blue and green.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: At night, with no sunlight, would the colour of your shirt still matter for warmth?
options: yes, white shirts glow softly at night
no, every shirt becomes equally cold
no, there is no sunlight to absorb or reflect
yes, black shirts make their own heat
questions.explanation: Colour matters only because dark colours absorb sunlight. Without sunlight there is nothing to absorb, so colour makes little difference.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: The Sun's heat evaporates water from
questions.explanation: Heat from the Sun evaporates water from oceans and lakes; the vapour rises and forms clouds.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: In the water cycle, water vapour rises, cools, forms clouds and falls back as
questions.explanation: The book says the vapour cools, forms clouds and falls back as rain.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: The water cycle would still exist even without heat.
questions.explanation: False. The book says the water cycle 'would not exist without heat' — heat drives evaporation.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: Winds form because
options: air moves when it is heated
questions.explanation: You learnt that air moves because of heat; this movement of air leads to winds.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: Ocean currents carry ___ across the planet.
questions.explanation: Heat drives ocean currents that carry warmth across the planet.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: Rocks slowly crack over time because they
options: float away in deep flood water
expand in heat and shrink in cold
questions.explanation: Heat shapes the land: rocks expand when heated and shrink when cold, slowly cracking.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: Monsoons are driven by
options: uneven heating of land and sea
even heating of the whole Earth
questions.explanation: The book says monsoons are driven by the uneven heating of land and sea.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: Without the Sun's heat, the Earth would be
questions.explanation: The book says without the Sun's heat, Earth would be a frozen, lifeless rock.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: Select ALL the things the book says are powered by the Sun's heat.
questions.explanation: Heat from the Sun evaporates water (water cycle) and moves air (winds). The Moon's light and earthquakes are not mentioned as effects of heat.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: Which is the correct order of steps in the water cycle as described in the book?
questions.explanation: Heat evaporates water, the vapour rises, cools, forms clouds, and falls back as rain.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: Every plant grows because of the Sun's heat.
questions.explanation: True. The book says every plant grows because of it and every animal depends on it.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: Why does a black car parked in the sun get hotter inside than a white car?
options: black paint is a better insulator
white paint makes its own cold
the dark colour absorbs more sunlight
questions.explanation: Dark-coloured objects absorb more sunlight and become hotter; light colours reflect sunlight.

questions.question: The layer of gases wrapped around the Earth is called the
questions.explanation: The Earth is wrapped in a layer of gases called the atmosphere.

questions.question: Some gases in the atmosphere trap the Sun's heat like a blanket. This is called the
questions.explanation: The natural trapping of heat by gases, keeping Earth warm enough for life, is the greenhouse effect.

questions.question: The greenhouse effect keeps the Earth
questions.explanation: The gases act like a blanket, keeping Earth warm enough for life.

questions.question: Which human activities add extra greenhouse gases to the atmosphere?
options: riding bicycles and walking to school
burning fuel and cutting down trees
questions.explanation: The book names burning fuel and cutting down trees as activities adding extra greenhouse gases.

questions.question: When extra gases trap more heat than needed and slowly make the Earth warmer, it is called
questions.explanation: Global warming is the extra warming caused by too many greenhouse gases trapping more heat than needed.

questions.question: Select ALL the effects of global warming listed in the book.
questions.explanation: Global warming causes ice to melt, sea level to rise and weather to become more extreme. It does not cool the Sun or freeze the oceans.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed as an effect of global warming?
questions.explanation: The listed effects are melting ice, rising sea level and more extreme weather.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the book's suggested ways to help?
questions.explanation: The book suggests saving electricity, planting trees and using bicycles or public transport.

questions.question: The greenhouse effect itself is harmful and the Earth would be better off without it.
questions.explanation: False. The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life. The problem is EXTRA gases trapping too much heat — that is global warming.

questions.question: Cutting down trees adds extra greenhouse gases to the atmosphere.
questions.explanation: True. The book lists cutting down trees, along with burning fuel, as adding extra greenhouse gases.

questions.question: What is the difference between the greenhouse effect and global warming?
options: they are simply two names for exactly the same thing
global warming is natural; the greenhouse effect is human-made
the greenhouse effect cools Earth; global warming heats it
natural warming vs extra warming caused by humans
questions.explanation: The greenhouse effect is the natural blanket that keeps Earth liveable. Global warming is the extra heating caused by humans adding more gases.

questions.question: Comparing the gases to a 'blanket' means that they
options: keep heat from escaping into space
questions.explanation: A blanket keeps your heat in; the gases trap the Sun's heat and stop it escaping.

questions.question: 'Small actions add up' means that
options: the Sun will fix the problem itself
everyday choices by each person matter
only big factories can make a change
questions.explanation: Each of us can help with small actions like saving electricity, planting trees and cycling.

questions.question: Using a bicycle or public transport helps slow global warming because it
options: cools down the Sun's hot rays
burns less fuel for each traveller
questions.explanation: Burning fuel adds greenhouse gases; cycling or sharing a bus burns far less fuel per person.

questions.question: Global warming is making weather more extreme.
questions.explanation: True. The book says global warming is causing ice to melt, sea level to rise and weather to become more extreme.

questions.question: The device used to measure how hot or cold something is, is a
questions.explanation: A thermometer gives an exact number for how hot or cold something is.

questions.question: Temperature is measured in a unit whose symbol is
questions.explanation: Temperature is measured in degree Celsius (°C). Kilograms, metres and litres measure mass, length and volume.

questions.question: The exact number a thermometer gives is called
questions.explanation: The thermometer's reading — like 37°C or 100°C — is called temperature.

questions.question: Which reading does the book give as an example of normal human body temperature?
questions.explanation: The book's example is 37°C for your body temperature and 100°C for boiling water.

questions.question: A thermometer in boiling water would read about
questions.explanation: Water boils at 100°C.

questions.question: What does a thermometer actually measure?
options: temperature, not the amount of heat
the amount of heat, not temperature
questions.explanation: A thermometer tells how hot or cold something is (temperature). It does not tell how much heat energy the object contains.

questions.question: A thermometer measures the total heat energy inside an object.
questions.explanation: False. A thermometer measures temperature (hotness level). Heat energy also depends on how much material there is.

questions.question: We cannot see or hold heat, but we can feel it and generate it.
questions.explanation: True. The book says exactly this before asking whether we can measure it too.

questions.question: You say a cup is 'hot' and your friend says 'very hot'. The better way to settle this is to
options: guess from the colour of the cup
read the temperature on a thermometer
touch the cup with both hands
ask more of your friends to touch it
questions.explanation: Feelings differ from person to person; a thermometer gives one exact number.

questions.question: Two identical containers of warm water, one half full and one full to the brim, are left for five minutes. Which cools faster?
options: both cool at exactly the same rate
the one filled to the brim
questions.explanation: The half-filled container has less water, so it holds less heat energy and cools faster.

questions.question: In the same investigation, which container was holding more heat energy at the start?
options: the one filled to the brim
questions.explanation: Both were at the same temperature, but the full container has more water, so it holds more heat energy.

questions.question: Why does the fuller container cool down more slowly?
options: it has more water, so more heat to lose
it started at a higher temperature
less air can touch its open surface
questions.explanation: Both started at the same temperature from the same flask. The fuller one simply contains more heat energy, so it takes longer to cool.

questions.question: The kilogram is a unit for measuring temperature.
questions.explanation: False. Kilogram measures mass. Temperature is measured in degree Celsius (°C).

questions.question: Which measurement would you make with a thermometer?
options: how long the soup spoon is
how hot a bowl of soup is
how heavy a bowl of soup is
how much soup is in the bowl
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures hotness or coldness — temperature.

questions.question: In the two-container investigation, why did both containers start at the same temperature?
options: they were left for five minutes
they were filled from the same flask
they were the same size and shape
questions.explanation: Both were filled with warm water from the same flask, so they began at equal temperature.

questions.question: Which of these is a correct temperature reading?
questions.explanation: Temperature uses degree Celsius (°C). kg, m and L measure mass, length and volume.

questions.question: Temperature tells us
options: how hot or cold something is
questions.explanation: Temperature is a measure of hotness or coldness; it does not tell us the amount of heat energy.

questions.question: Heat is best described as
questions.explanation: Heat is energy. Temperature is the number that tells how hot or cold something is.

questions.question: Water boils at 100°C. This boiling temperature is
options: lower for a small cup of water
the same for any amount of water
higher for a bigger pot of water
questions.explanation: Temperature does not depend on amount: water boils at 100°C whether you have a cup or a pool.

questions.question: A large pot of water and a small cup of water are both at 70°C. Which contains more heat energy?
options: the cup, because it is smaller
both contain the same heat energy
neither, heat and temperature are the same
the pot, because it has more water
questions.explanation: Same temperature, but the pot has far more water, so it contains far more heat energy.

questions.question: Why do you need far more heat to warm a swimming pool than a cup of water to the same temperature?
options: the pool contains much more water
the pool is always kept outdoors
the cup is made of thin metal
questions.explanation: Heat depends on amount of material: more water needs more heat energy to reach the same temperature.

questions.question: A large swimming pool and a cup of water at the same temperature contain the same amount of heat.
questions.explanation: False. They are at the same temperature, but the pool holds far more heat because it contains much more water.

questions.question: Temperature tells us how much heat energy an object contains.
questions.explanation: False. Temperature only tells how hot or cold something is. The heat energy also depends on how much material there is.

questions.question: Clue: 'A thermometer reads 37°C for any healthy human body, child or adult.' This clue describes
options: temperature — the same reading no matter the size
heat — bigger bodies give higher readings
heat — grown adults store up more warmth
questions.explanation: The reading is the same regardless of body size, which is how temperature behaves — it does not depend on amount.

questions.question: Clue: 'A big pot of soup takes much longer to heat up than a small cup, even on the same flame.' This clue describes
options: temperature — the cup boils at a lower number
heat — more soup needs more energy
questions.explanation: The bigger pot needs more heat energy to reach the same temperature, so the clue is about heat.

questions.question: Clue: 'Ice cream melts at 0°C, the same number for a scoop or a full tub.' This clue describes
options: heat — the tub needs no energy to melt
heat — the scoop holds more energy
temperature — the tub melts at a higher number
temperature — amount does not change it
questions.explanation: The melting point is the same number for any amount, which is a property of temperature.

questions.question: A pool and a cup of water at the same temperature feel equally warm to touch. What does touching tell you?
options: the temperature, not the amount of heat
the amount of heat, not the temperature
both the heat and the temperature
how many particles are in the water
questions.explanation: Touch senses how hot something is (temperature). It cannot tell you that the pool holds far more heat energy than the cup.

questions.question: Two cups of tea and one cup of tea are all at 60°C. Which is correct?
options: the single cup holds more heat energy
two cups together hold more heat than one
one cup is hotter than the two cups
all of them hold equal heat energy
questions.explanation: Same temperature, but twice the tea means twice the material and so more heat energy.

questions.question: Which pair is matched correctly?
options: heat → how hot something is; temperature → energy
heat → energy; temperature → how hot something is
questions.explanation: Heat is energy; temperature is the measure of hotness, read in degree Celsius on a thermometer.

questions.question: A big pot and a small cup of water are placed on identical flames. Which reaches 70°C first?
options: both at exactly the same time
questions.explanation: The cup has less water, so it needs less heat energy to reach 70°C and gets there first.

questions.question: Water boils at 100°C whether it is in a small kettle or a large pot.
questions.explanation: True. Boiling temperature does not depend on the amount of water.

questions.question: The statement 'Heat and temperature mean the same thing' is
options: false — heat is energy, temperature is hotness
true — they are two words for one idea
true, but only when talking about water
false — they are both measuring devices
questions.explanation: People often mix them up, but heat is energy while temperature tells how hot or cold something is.

questions.question: A tub of ice cream and a scoop of ice cream both melt at 0°C. Which needs MORE heat to melt completely?
questions.explanation: Same melting temperature, but the tub has far more ice cream, so more heat energy is needed to melt it all.

questions.question: The temperature of a healthy human body stays close to
questions.explanation: A healthy human body stays close to 37°C.

questions.question: Our body produces heat through
questions.explanation: The book says our body makes heat through every breath, every move and every meal we digest.

questions.question: A slight rise above 37°C tells the doctor that
options: the immune system is fighting infection
the body is becoming far too cold
the patient has not eaten any food
questions.explanation: A slight fever means the immune system is actively fighting an infection.

questions.question: A clinical or digital thermometer is placed
options: on the sole of the bare foot
under the tongue or in the armpit
on the top of the forehead only
in the palm of the open hand
questions.explanation: Doctors and nurses place it under the tongue or in the armpit for an accurate reading.

questions.question: Infrared thermometers are used in emergencies and epidemics because they
options: are the most accurate of all
must be held under the tongue
questions.explanation: Infrared thermometers quickly check people's temperature without touching them.

questions.question: The body's work of keeping its temperature steady at about 37°C is called
questions.explanation: Thermoregulation is how our bodies constantly stay at 37°C — not too hot, not too cold.

questions.question: When we get too hot, we
questions.explanation: Sweating cools the body down when it gets too hot.

questions.question: When we get too cold, our body makes us
questions.explanation: Shivering is the body's way of generating heat when it is cold.

questions.question: Shivering warms the body because
options: blood stops flowing to the skin
the body hair grows much thicker
muscles move rapidly to generate heat
the skin releases drops of water
questions.explanation: When we shiver, our muscles move rapidly and this movement generates heat.

questions.question: Select ALL the things that happen when we get TOO HOT.
questions.explanation: Too hot: we sweat and feel thirsty. Shivering and goose-bumps happen when we are too cold.

questions.question: Select ALL the things that happen when we get TOO COLD.
questions.explanation: Too cold: we shiver and get goose-bumps. Sweating and thirst are responses to being too hot.

questions.question: A very high fever must be brought down carefully because too much heat
questions.explanation: The book says getting too hot affects brain function, which is why a very high fever must be brought down carefully.

questions.question: Sweating is the body's way of warming itself up.
questions.explanation: False. Sweating cools the body down when it is too hot. Shivering warms it up.

questions.question: Dressing warmly helps our body conserve its heat.
questions.explanation: True. Warm clothes are insulators that help the body keep the heat it makes.

questions.question: Honeybees vibrating their flight muscles to make heat is most like a human
questions.explanation: The book says the bees do exactly what our body does when it shivers — rapid muscle movement generates heat.

questions.question: Our body temperature changes a lot between a hot summer day and a cold winter morning.
questions.explanation: False. Our body stays at almost the same temperature (about 37°C) in summer and winter thanks to thermoregulation.

questions.question: One of the first things a doctor does when you are unwell is
questions.explanation: Measuring temperature tells the doctor whether your body is fighting an infection.

questions.question: Goose-bumps appear when we are
questions.explanation: Goose-bumps are listed among the body's responses to getting too cold.

questions.question: Water freezes at
questions.explanation: Water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C.

questions.question: A fridge keeps food fresh at about
questions.explanation: A fridge stays at about 4°C to keep food fresh.

questions.question: An oven bakes bread and cakes at around
questions.explanation: An oven heats up to around 180°C to bake bread and cakes.

questions.question: Our bodies feel most comfortable between
questions.explanation: The comfortable range for our bodies is 20°C to 28°C.

questions.question: If the room temperature drops well below 20°C, you are most likely to
questions.explanation: Below the comfortable 20°C–28°C range we feel cold and reach for a sweater; above it we reach for a cooler.

questions.question: Cooking vegetables at very high heat for too long can destroy important
questions.explanation: The book warns that very high heat for too long destroys vitamins like Vitamin C.

questions.question: Which cooking method helps keep more nutrients in vegetables?
options: deep frying for a long time
questions.explanation: Steaming or lightly cooking vegetables keeps more nutrients intact.

questions.question: According to the book, our body digests food best when it
questions.explanation: The book says our body digests best when it stays warm.

questions.question: Drinking enough water is important for health only if the water is warm.
questions.explanation: False. Whether you prefer warm or cool water, drinking ENOUGH water is what matters for digestion and good health.

questions.question: Emperor penguins in Antarctica huddle through snowstorms that reach
questions.explanation: The snowstorms reach −60°C, so the penguins huddle tightly together.

questions.question: Every few minutes the penguins rotate. This means
options: centre penguins move out and outer ones move in
the centre penguins stay in the centre
outer penguins walk away from the group
all the penguins turn to face the wind
questions.explanation: Those from the warm centre shuffle to the cold edge, and the cold ones move inward — no penguin keeps the warmth to itself.

questions.question: Why does the penguin huddle as a whole stay warm even though individual penguins move around?
options: penguins stop producing body heat when they huddle together
huddled bodies share heat and are less exposed to cold
the penguin in the centre makes heat for the whole group
the snow around the huddle keeps all the heat inside
questions.explanation: Each penguin's body heat warms its neighbours, and the tight huddle leaves less surface open to the freezing wind; rotating shares the warm spots.

questions.question: What would happen if the penguins in the centre never moved outward?
options: the whole group would quickly overheat
nothing would change for the group
the outer penguins would become dangerously cold
every penguin would stay equally warm
questions.explanation: The outer penguins face the full storm. If they were never allowed into the centre, they would lose too much heat.

questions.question: The honeybees raise the temperature inside their ball to about
questions.explanation: By vibrating their flight muscles, the bees raise the ball's temperature to about 47°C.

questions.question: The hornet cannot survive beyond
questions.explanation: The hornet cannot survive beyond 46°C, while the bees can survive up to 48°C.

questions.question: The honeybees can survive up to
questions.explanation: Bees survive up to 48°C, two degrees above the hornet's limit of 46°C.

questions.question: The bees generate heat inside the ball by
options: fanning in cool air with wings
questions.explanation: Hundreds of bees vibrate their flight muscles at the same time, generating heat through movement.

questions.question: The bees heat the ball to about 47°C. This is just one degree above
questions.explanation: The hornet dies beyond 46°C; the ball reaches 47°C — 'one degree of difference and the bees know exactly where that line is'.

questions.question: The honeybees kill the hornet by stinging it many times.
questions.explanation: False. No sting, no crush — just heat generated through movement.

questions.question: The hornet trapped inside the bee ball can still breathe.
questions.explanation: True. The bees do not crush it and it can still breathe, yet it dies from the heat.

questions.question: Which statement about the bee ball is NOT true?
options: the hornet is frozen to death
the bees do not sting it
the bees do not crush it
questions.explanation: The hornet is killed by HEAT, not cold — the ball reaches about 47°C.

questions.question: Which is colder: a fridge at 4°C or ice water at 0°C?
questions.explanation: 0°C is lower than 4°C, so ice water is colder than the inside of the fridge.

questions.question: Which of these temperatures is closest to a comfortable room for humans?
questions.explanation: Humans feel most comfortable between 20°C and 28°C; 24°C is in that range. 4°C is fridge-cold, 37°C is body heat, 47°C is the bee ball.

questions.question: The penguins on the outside of the huddle face the full force of the storm.
questions.explanation: True. Those on the outside face the full storm while those at the centre stay warm.

questions.question: In India, summer lasts from
questions.explanation: The book's season chart shows Summer as March–June.

questions.question: In summer, temperatures in most parts of India soar to
questions.explanation: Summer temperatures soar to 35°C–48°C; days are long and the air is dry.

questions.question: The hot winds that sweep across the plains in summer are called
questions.explanation: Hot winds called loo sweep across the plains in summer.

questions.question: The monsoon season in India is
questions.explanation: The chart shows Monsoon as July–September.

questions.question: During the monsoon, rain brings temperatures down to
questions.explanation: Monsoon: temperatures 25°C–35°C, humid and sticky air, rivers fill up.

questions.question: Autumn (October–November) brings temperatures of
questions.explanation: In autumn temperature falls to 20°C–30°C and the weather turns comfortable and crisp.

questions.question: Which set of events belongs to AUTUMN in the book's chart?
options: mornings are foggy, nights are long
leaves fall, birds migrate, farmers harvest
rivers fill, frogs emerge, seeds are planted
hot winds blow, days are long, air is dry
questions.explanation: Autumn: leaves start falling, birds migrate and farmers harvest their crops.

questions.question: In winter, the plains of India cool to
questions.explanation: Winter: plains cool to 5°C–20°C while mountains drop below −20°C.

questions.question: In which season do frogs emerge and farmers plant seeds?
questions.explanation: During the monsoon rivers fill up, frogs emerge and farmers plant seeds.

questions.question: According to the book, a season is
options: a change in heat reaching us over the year
a change in the number of days in a month
a change in the Sun's own temperature
a change in the Earth's inner heat
questions.explanation: A season is what happens when the amount of heat reaching us changes slowly over an entire year.

questions.question: Indian farmers sow wheat in
questions.explanation: Wheat is sown in October–November and harvested in March.

questions.question: Why is wheat sown when the weather turns cooler?
options: rain is heaviest at that time of year
the Sun is strongest in those months
cooler soil slows bacteria and lets roots grow
the hot loo winds help the seeds sprout
questions.explanation: Cooler temperatures slow bacterial growth in the soil and give the seeds time to establish roots.

questions.question: Wheat is harvested in
questions.explanation: Wheat is harvested in March before the summer heat arrives.

questions.question: Rice is planted in the rainy season (June–July) because it needs
questions.explanation: Rice needs lots of water and warm temperatures, so it is planted in the rainy season.

questions.question: Rice is harvested in
questions.explanation: Rice is planted in June–July and harvested in autumn.

questions.question: An early winter, a delayed monsoon or a long heat wave can
questions.explanation: When seasonal temperatures shift unexpectedly, crop yields can be severely affected.

questions.question: Absolute zero is
questions.explanation: Absolute zero, the coldest possible temperature, is −273°C.

questions.question: Absolute zero is best described as
options: the freezing point of pure water
the temperature of a normal fridge
questions.explanation: Scientists discovered a coldest possible temperature — nothing anywhere can ever be colder.

questions.question: As something gets colder and colder towards absolute zero, its particles
questions.explanation: Heat comes from particles moving; the colder something is, the slower its particles move.

questions.question: Arrange from coldest to hottest: boiling water, absolute zero, ice water, human body.
options: absolute zero, human body, ice water, boiling water
ice water, human body, absolute zero, boiling water
absolute zero, ice water, human body, boiling water
ice water, absolute zero, human body, boiling water
questions.explanation: −273°C (absolute zero) < 0°C (ice water) < 37°C (body) < 100°C (boiling water).

questions.question: How much colder is absolute zero than ice water at 0°C?
questions.explanation: Absolute zero is −273°C, which is 273 degrees below 0°C.

questions.question: Nothing in the universe can be colder than absolute zero.
questions.explanation: True. Absolute zero (−273°C) is the coldest possible temperature; nothing can ever be colder.

questions.question: In winter, mountain temperatures in India drop below −2°C according to the book.
questions.explanation: False. The book says mountains drop below −20°C in winter, not −2°C.

questions.question: In the 'Moli the Molecule' comic, panel 4 shows Moli
questions.explanation: Panel 1 is room temperature, panel 2 near freezing, panel 3 very deep cold, panel 4 approaching absolute zero.

questions.question: Rice grows best in cool, dry conditions.
questions.explanation: False. Rice needs lots of water and warm temperatures, which is why it is planted in the rainy season.

questions.question: The coldest winter day in a city is 5°C. Compared with absolute zero, this day is
questions.explanation: From −273°C up to 5°C is 273 + 5 = 278 degrees.

questions.question: Which two numbers 'shape how we cook, store food and even what weather feels like'?
questions.explanation: Water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C; these two numbers shape cooking, food storage and weather.

questions.question: Understanding temperature and climate is described as the foundation of feeding a nation.
questions.explanation: True. The book says understanding temperature and climate 'is the foundation of feeding a nation'.

questions.question: Select ALL the things that are true about the particles inside an object.
options: they are too small to see
they stop moving when the object is cold
they are only found in hot objects
questions.explanation: Particles are too small to see and constantly bump into each other. They keep moving even when cold, and every object has them.

questions.question: Select ALL the places the book links with heat coming from inside the Earth.
questions.explanation: Puga Valley and Beppu both have hot springs heated by the Earth's interior. Antarctica is mentioned for penguins, and the Sun is not geothermal.

questions.question: Select ALL the appliances the book lists as converting electrical energy into heat.
questions.explanation: Electric heaters, ovens, geysers and room heaters convert electricity into heat. Campfires and gas stoves burn fuel; a bicycle is not a heat source.

questions.topic: Heat Flows from Hot to Cold
questions.question: A cold spoon is placed in warm water. Select ALL the statements that are correct.
options: heat flows from the water into the spoon
the spoon warms up and the water cools a little
heat flows from the spoon into the water
the water gets hotter than before
questions.explanation: Heat flows from hotter (water) to cooler (spoon), so the spoon warms and the water cools slightly. It never flows the other way.

questions.question: Select ALL the objects that would make a GOOD handle for a hot pan.
questions.explanation: Wood and plastic are insulators and stay cool; iron and copper are metal conductors that would get hot.

questions.topic: Heat Through Moving Matter and Empty Space
questions.question: Select ALL the examples of heat travelling through EMPTY SPACE.
options: a campfire warming your face from a distance
a heater warming a room's air
a spoon warming in hot tea
questions.explanation: Sun and campfire heat reach you as rays without contact. The heater uses moving air; the spoon is heat through touch.

questions.topic: Colour, Sunlight and Heat in Nature
questions.question: Select ALL the ways the book says heat shapes the land and weather.
options: rocks crack from expanding and shrinking
monsoons come from uneven heating of land and sea
questions.explanation: The book says rocks crack as they expand in heat and shrink in cold, and monsoons are driven by uneven heating. The other two are not in the book.

questions.question: Select ALL the actions the book suggests to help slow global warming.
questions.explanation: The book suggests saving electricity, planting trees and using bicycles or public transport. Burning fuel and cutting trees make it worse.

questions.question: Select ALL the readings that a thermometer could sensibly show for the things named.
questions.explanation: Water boils at 100°C and a healthy body is close to 37°C. The other two pairs swap the numbers.

questions.question: A swimming pool and a cup of water are at the same temperature. Select ALL the TRUE statements.
options: the pool contains more heat energy
both feel equally warm to the touch
the cup contains more heat energy
the pool is at a higher temperature
questions.explanation: Same temperature means they feel equally warm, but the pool holds far more heat because it has much more water.

questions.question: Select ALL the thermometers the book says doctors and nurses use on people.
questions.explanation: Clinical/digital thermometers go under the tongue or in the armpit; infrared thermometers check people without contact.

questions.question: Select ALL the statements that are true about emperor penguins in the book.
options: penguins from the centre move to the outside edge
one leader penguin signals when to rotate
the outside penguins never get a turn in the centre
questions.explanation: They huddle through −60°C storms and rotate without any signal or leader, so every penguin gets a turn in the warm centre.

questions.question: Select ALL the correct crop-and-season pairs from the book.
questions.explanation: Wheat is sown in the cooler months (October–November); rice is planted in the rainy season (June–July).

questions.question: Select ALL the temperatures from the book that are COLDER than ice water (0°C).
questions.explanation: Negative temperatures are below 0°C, so −60°C and −20°C are colder than ice water. 4°C and 5°C are warmer than 0°C.
